result:
The proposed answer of 1/2 is incorrect. The correct limit is r/(r+1).

**Why 1/2 is not the maximum.** Write each S-smooth integer as an exponent vector x = (a_1, …, a_r). The forbidden pattern says that n and all of its r "up-neighbors" p_i·n cannot lie in A together. So A is valid exactly when every x ∈ A has at least one up-neighbor x + e_i outside A. Let B = M(S) ∖ A.

**Upper bound.** Each x ∈ A needs some up-neighbor in B. Each b ∈ B has at most r down-neighbors. So |A| ≤ r·|B| up to boundary terms near X, which are negligible. Hence the density of A is at most r/(r+1).

**Lower bound (construction).** Let B = {x : Σ i·a_i ≡ 0 (mod r+1)}. For x ∉ B with residue c ∈ {1, …, r}, the element x + e_i has residue c + i. Choosing i = r+1−c ∈ {1, …, r} gives residue 0, so x + e_i ∈ B. Thus every element of A has an up-neighbor in B, and A avoids the pattern. B has density 1/(r+1), assuming the residues mod (r+1) are asymptotically equidistributed among S-smooth numbers, which holds for the counting function. So A has density r/(r+1).

**Check for r = 2.** B = {x : a_1 + 2a_2 ≡ 0 (mod 3)} has density 1/3, and its complement has density 2/3 > 1/2. For x ∈ A, if the residue is 1 then x + e_2 lies in B, and if it is 2 then x + e_1 lies in B. So the pattern {n, p_1 n, p_2 n} is never fully contained in A.

The proposed argument only shows that the parity-of-exponent set achieves 1/2, which is a lower bound, and then asserts without justification that 1/2 is optimal. That assertion is false. The r = 1 case (limit 1/2) is consistent with the general formula r/(r+1).

VERDICT: REJECT
CONFIDENCE: 4
